titleStmt.title: Parvalbumin-Expressing Inhibitory Interneurons in Auditory Cortex Are Well-Tuned for Frequency
titleStmt.author: Moore
Wehr

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Parvalbumin-Expressing Inhibitory Interneurons in Auditory Cortex Are Well-Tuned for Frequency

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: what the receptive fields of a genetically defined inhibitory cell class actually look like, as opposed to what is inferred from blocking inhibition wholesale
span.quote: Pharmacological and whole-cell voltage-clamp studies have indicated important computational functions for cortical inhibition, such as shaping receptive fields, enhancing temporal precision, and providing gain control ( Wang et al., 2002b ; Wehr and Zador, 2003 ; Tan et al., 2004 ; Wu et al., 2006 ). However, these methods lump together all sources of synaptic inhibition, and thus cannot reveal the distinct contributions of specific subtypes of inhibitory neurons. To reveal their specific contributions, direct measurement of the tuning properties of each inhibitory cell type is necessary.

span.label: whether and how the response properties of PV+ neurons differ from those of PV- neurons in auditory cortex
span.quote: The morphological and physiological diversity of interneurons suggests that these different subclasses have unique roles in sound processing; however, these roles are yet unknown. Understanding the receptive field properties of distinct inhibitory cell types will be critical to elucidating their computational function in cortical circuits.

span.label: auditory cortical PV+ neurons are well tuned for frequency, unlike their visual cortical counterparts, which is what the local-pooling account predicts given tonotopy
span.quote: In contrast to PV+ neurons in mouse visual cortex, which are broadly tuned for orientation, we found that auditory cortical PV+ neurons were well tuned for frequency, although very tightly tuned PV+ cells were uncommon. This suggests that PV+ neurons play a minor role in shaping frequency tuning, and is consistent with the idea that PV+ neurons nonselectively pool input from the local network.

span.label: existence
span.quote: In contrast to PV+ neurons in mouse visual cortex, which are broadly tuned for orientation, we found that auditory cortical PV+ neurons were well tuned for frequency, although very tightly tuned PV+ cells were uncommon.

span.label: frequency tuning of parvalbumin-positive interneurons in auditory cortex
span.quote: Here we characterized the tuning and response properties of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons, the largest inhibitory subclass.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We obtained single-unit extracellular recordings from optogenetically identified PV+ neurons in mice that expressed ChR2 specifically in PV+ cells.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PV+ interneurons pool densely and without bias from excitatory neurons in a small local radius, so their tuning inherits the feature organization of that local patch - homogeneous in a columnar or tonotopic area, heterogeneous in a salt-and-pepper one
span.quote: Because PV+ neurons densely sample a small radius, their tuning is expected to reflect feature organization in local networks: in orientation columns in cat V1 and vibrissa barrels in rodent S1, PV+ cells will sample inputs with homogeneous tuning, and thus themselves will be well tuned

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Greater monotonicity keeps PV+ firing rates rising over a wider span of sound levels, which stretches the level dynamic range and thereby flattens the slope of the rate-level function
span.quote: Moreover, Δ dB was correlated with MI ( r = 0.377, p < 0.01), suggesting that the greater monotonicity of PV+ neurons is responsible for their increased dynamic range in sound level, and thus their comparatively shallow response gain.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Faster membrane time constants combined with strong thalamocortical synaptic drive make PV+ cells fire early, placing them in a feedforward inhibitory loop that sharpens the timing of pyramidal responses
span.quote: The rapid activation of PV+ neurons may arise from faster membrane time constants ( Cardin et al., 2007 ) in combination with potent thalamocortical synaptic drive ( Swadlow, 2003 ), as has been shown for FS cells in V1 and S1, respectively.

span.label: PV+ cells densely sample a small radius, so their tuning should mirror how the local network is organised - broad where tuning is salt-and-pepper, narrow where it is columnar
span.quote: Because PV+ neurons densely sample a small radius, their tuning is expected to reflect feature organization in local networks: in orientation columns in cat V1 and vibrissa barrels in rodent S1, PV+ cells will sample inputs with homogeneous tuning, and thus themselves will be well tuned ( Simons, 1978 ; Hirsch et al., 2003 ; Cardin et al., 2007 ; Nowak et al., 2008 ). In contrast, PV+ neurons are found to be poorly tuned where cells with different stimulus preferences are organized in a salt-and-pepper fashion, as in mouse V1, which lacks orientation columns

span.label: cotuned inhibition sharpens spike tuning through a thresholding or iceberg mechanism rather than by suppressing non-preferred stimuli
span.quote: More recently, voltage-clamp studies have shown that excitation and inhibition are instead cotuned for frequency and approximately fixed in their relative proportions ( Wehr and Zador, 2003 ; Zhang et al., 2003 ; Tan et al., 2004 ; for review see Oswald et al., 2006 ). In the cotuning model, inhibition moderately sharpens spike tuning through a thresholding or “iceberg” mechanism, scaling down depolarization across the same range of frequencies as excitation.

span.label: very short PV+ latencies suggest a feedforward inhibitory network driven rapidly by thalamocortical excitation
span.quote: We found that PV+ neurons had markedly faster response latencies than PV− neurons. These very short latencies suggest that PV+ neurons participate in a feedforward inhibitory network that is rapidly activated by thalamocortical excitation, and likely underlies the sequence of early synaptic excitation and inhibition seen in whole-cell recordings from pyramidal neurons

span.label: monotonic PV+ rate-level functions support local inhibition shaping intensity tuning in auditory cortex
span.quote: We found that PV+ neurons were highly monotonic for pure tones at their characteristic frequency compared with PV− neurons. This supports the idea that local inhibition shapes intensity tuning in auditory cortex, and that it is provided at least in part by PV+ neurons.

span.label: the pooling and feedforward roles could be performed in sequence, or simultaneously for continuous sounds
span.quote: Is a role in providing rapid feedforward inhibition compatible with the local pooling hypothesis? PV+ neurons could play both roles, perhaps sequentially. After providing an initial volley of feedforward inhibition, PV+ neurons could then pool activity from the local cortical network and provide ongoing feedback inhibition. Both roles could be performed simultaneously for continuous acoustic streams.

span.label: Not every stimulus set could be run on every cell, so the sub-samples for tuning curves, rate-level functions and latency differ.
span.quote: Due to the constraints of recording duration, we were not able to present all stimulus arrays for all cells.

span.label: The PV− comparison group is only presumed to be excitatory; a small fraction could be non-PV inhibitory interneurons.
span.quote: Presumably, these PV− cells were almost exclusively excitatory pyramidal cells, although a small fraction (<12%; Meyer et al., 2011 ; Xu et al., 2010 ) could have been PV− inhibitory interneurons.

span.label: The observed heterogeneity of PV+ response properties may partly reflect limited specificity of the PV promoter rather than true biological diversity.
span.quote: This is likely due at least in part to the degree of specificity of the PV promoter, which expresses in more than one cell type, but may also arise from heterogeneity within cell types as well.

span.label: well tuned PV+ cells are also consistent with selective connectivity rather than unbiased pooling, though that would be a different rule from other cortical areas
span.quote: We note that well tuned PV+ neurons are also consistent with selective connectivity rather than unbiased pooling, because narrow tuning could follow from either scheme. However, this would represent a different connectivity rule than is found in other cortical areas.

span.label: lateral inhibition could still operate here, either through a different network configuration or through other inhibitory cell types
span.quote: Nevertheless, lateral inhibition could still be implemented in auditory cortex in at least two ways. First, recent modeling studies have shown that a single network architecture (which is consistent with our results) can operate in either a cotuned or lateral inhibition configuration, depending on the strength and spatial profile of thalamic input ( Levy and Reyes, 2011 ). Second, other inhibitory cell types could participate in classical lateral inhibition.

span.label: a small fraction of the PV- sample could have been non-PV inhibitory interneurons rather than pyramidal cells
span.quote: Presumably, these PV− cells were almost exclusively excitatory pyramidal cells, although a small fraction (<12%; Meyer et al., 2011 ; Xu et al., 2010 ) could have been PV− inhibitory interneurons.

span.label: recording duration prevented presenting every stimulus array to every cell, so the two samples are only approximately matched
span.quote: Due to the constraints of recording duration, we were not able to present all stimulus arrays for all cells. Stimuli presented to our PV− sample were approximately matched to the PV+ sample.

span.label: deep-layer neurons were slightly underrepresented relative to the anatomical distribution
span.quote: The distribution of depths for our electrophysiologically recorded PV+ neurons did not differ significantly from the distribution of tdTomato-expressing cells (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p > 0.05), although neurons in deep layers were slightly underrepresented in our sample.

span.label: the unbiased local pooling principle, carried across modalities as a prediction that reverses because auditory cortex is columnar where mouse V1 is not
span.quote: If this principle generalizes across sensory modalities, PV+ neurons in mouse auditory cortex should be well tuned for frequency, because it has tonotopically organized frequency columns.

span.label: the monotonicity index and rate-level function decomposition, used to give intensity tuning a single number
span.quote: Monotonicity index (MI) characterizes the strength of a cell's intensity tuning. We defined MI as the neuron's response at maximum intensity (90 dB) divided by its maximum response ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ). An MI of 1 indicates no intensity tuning; an MI near zero indicates very strong intensity tuning.

span.label: rate-level functions NORMALISED before comparison
span.quote: We therefore normalized rate-level functions to control for the higher firing rates in PV+ neurons.

span.label: PV+ here means a cell that responded to blue light with a reliable short-latency burst, in a mouse where over 97 percent of PV-immunopositive cells carry the opsin - identity by manipulation, validated against a stain in two separate reporter lines
span.quote: More than 97% of PV+ cells expressed ChR2-eYFP, as indicated by fluorescent immunostaining for PV ( Fig. 1 b ; n = 657 cells in two mice, four sections total). YFP-fluorescent somata were difficult to distinguish from neuropil because the ChR2-eYFP fusion protein is membrane-bound. To better quantify the distribution of PV+ cells in auditory cortex we crossed Pvalb -IRES-Cre to a cre-dependent tdTomato reporter line ( Madisen et al., 2010 ). Expression specificity was similar for the cytosolic tdTomato reporter: >97% of tdTomato-expressing cells stained positively for PV; >96% of PV-positive cells expressed tdTomato ( Fig. 1 c ; n = 638 cells in one mouse, four sections).

span.label: the FS/RS spike-width cutoff of 0.8 ms was set from THIS dataset, halfway between the two group means, and the paper states there is no consensus value in the literature because it may depend on the recording technology
span.quote: To separate fast-spiking (FS) from regular-spiking (RS) cells based on spike width alone, we used an empirically determined value of 0.8 ms, which was approximately halfway between the mean spike widths of our PV+ and PV− groups and provided the best separation between them. There does not appear to be a consensus value for the extracellular FS/RS spike width cutoff in the literature ( Atencio and Schreiner, 2008 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Wu et al., 2008 ) because it may depend on the choice of recording technology.

span.label: UNTUNED is a category created because the measure does not apply: a sound-responsive cell with disordered frequency-intensity structure has no meaningful tuning width, so it is labelled rather than fitted
span.quote: For this untuned but sound-responsive neuron, a Gaussian fit provided a poor estimate of tuning width ( Fig. 2 d ; R 2 = 0.04); indeed, the notion of tuning width seems inappropriate to describe such a neuron, and we therefore categorized this neuron as untuned (UT).

span.label: monotonicity index is a ratio of the response at the loudest tested level to the maximum response, so 1 means no intensity tuning and near zero means strong tuning - the measure carries its own null
span.quote: Monotonicity index (MI) characterizes the strength of a cell's intensity tuning. We defined MI as the neuron's response at maximum intensity (90 dB) divided by its maximum response ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ). An MI of 1 indicates no intensity tuning; an MI near zero indicates very strong intensity tuning.

span.label: the 80 ms response window was chosen to exclude non-evoked spikes BECAUSE PV+ cells have high spontaneous rates - an analysis choice driven by one of the very differences under study
span.quote: We chose this response window to best exclude non-stimulus-evoked spikes, because PV+ cells had high spontaneous firing rates.

span.label: contradicts → Wu et al. (2008), FS cells in rat A1
span.quote: This was also true when we separated cells according to spike width, which is inconsistent with a previous study of FS cells in rat A1 ( Wu et al., 2008 ).

span.label: builds-on → local-pooling account of PV+ tuning (Kerlin et al., 2010; Hofer et al., 2011)
span.quote: Our finding that the tuning widths of PV+ and PV− neurons were not significantly different is consistent with the idea that PV+ cells nonselectively “pool” input from local excitatory neurons ( Kerlin et al., 2010 ; Hofer et al., 2011 ).

span.label: replicates → Atencio and Schreiner (2008), FS cells in auditory cortex
span.quote: This is consistent with a previous study of FS cells in auditory cortex ( Atencio and Schreiner, 2008 ).

span.label: contradicts → lateral inhibition models in which sharpening comes from inhibitory neurons more broadly tuned than excitatory ones
span.quote: Lateral inhibition models propose that inhibition sharpens spike tuning by specifically inhibiting responses to nonpreferred stimuli ( Calford and Semple, 1995 ; Chen and Jen, 2000 ; Sutter and Loftus, 2003 ). This could be implemented by PV+ neurons that are more broadly tuned than excitatory neurons ( Wu et al., 2008 ), but our finding that PV+ and PV− neurons have similar tuning widths is inconsistent with this model.

span.label: supports → the cotuning model in which excitation and inhibition share frequency tuning and inhibition sharpens by thresholding
span.quote: Together, our results therefore favor a model of cotuning of PV+ neurons, produced by unbiased local connectivity, in which PV+-mediated inhibition has only a moderate impact on frequency tuning.

span.label: extends → the local unbiased pooling account of PV+ tuning developed in mouse visual cortex
span.quote: If this principle generalizes across sensory modalities, PV+ neurons in mouse auditory cortex should be well tuned for frequency, because it has tonotopically organized frequency columns.

span.label: critiques → the use of extracellular spike waveform as a marker for PV+ interneurons in vivo
span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons. These results suggest that both PV+ and FS cells are heterogeneous populations that overlap but are not identical.

span.label: qualifies → pharmacological and voltage-clamp studies that lump all sources of synaptic inhibition together
span.quote: Pharmacological and whole-cell voltage-clamp studies have indicated important computational functions for cortical inhibition, such as shaping receptive fields, enhancing temporal precision, and providing gain control ( Wang et al., 2002b ; Wehr and Zador, 2003 ; Tan et al., 2004 ; Wu et al., 2006 ). However, these methods lump together all sources of synaptic inhibition, and thus cannot reveal the distinct contributions of specific subtypes of inhibitory neurons. To reveal their specific contributions, direct measurement of the tuning properties of each inhibitory cell type is necessary.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE `because` INTRODUCES A PREMISE, AND THE EDGE READS IT AS A CONSEQUENCE) · local pooling —causes→ tonotopically
span.note: RETRACTED: THE `because` INTRODUCES A PREMISE, AND THE EDGE READS IT AS A CONSEQUENCE. The edge is `local pooling --causes--> tonotopically`. The span: 'BECAUSE mouse auditory cortex IS TONOTOPICALLY ORGANIZED, the local pooling hypothesis PREDICTS that PV+ cells, like PV- cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency.' Tonotopy is a BACKGROUND FACT the hypothesis is applied to; it is the given, not the product. Local pooling does not organise the cortex tonotopically - the tonotopy is what makes the pooling hypothesis yield a testable prediction about TUNING. WHAT THE SPAN DOES SAY (Q-309): that a known organisation plus a hypothesis yields a prediction, and the prediction is about tuning width, not about tonotopy. That is the sibling edge [2] `local pooling --causes--> tuning width`, which was READ IN THE SAME PASS AND LEFT - it has the prediction and the confirming result ('we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV- cells were not significantly different'). So nothing is kept here; the content is already carried by the edge next to it. — strength of the relation: 1 — THE PREDICTION REVERSES ACROSS MODALITIES: the same pooling principle makes PV+ cells broadly tuned in salt-and-pepper mouse V1 and well tuned in columnar auditory cortex
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: PV+ —contrasted-with→ visual cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the same cell class gives OPPOSITE tuning answers in two modalities, and that is the result rather than a discrepancy
span.quote: In contrast to PV+ neurons in mouse visual cortex, which are broadly tuned for orientation, we found that auditory cortical PV+ neurons were well tuned for frequency, although very tightly tuned PV+ cells were uncommon. This suggests that PV+ neurons play a minor role in shaping frequency tuning, and is consistent with the idea that PV+ neurons nonselectively pool input from the local network.

span.label: local pooling —causes→ tuning width
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — MECHANISM: dense sampling of a small radius means the cell inherits whatever tuning organisation that radius has - so a tonotopic area predicts well-tuned inhibitory cells
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: RETRACTED (A PREDICTION CONFIRMED BY A NULL, RECORDED AS A CONTRAST) · PV+ —contrasted-with→ PV−
span.note: RETRACTED: A PREDICTION CONFIRMED BY A NULL, RECORDED AS A CONTRAST. The edge is `PV+ --contrasted-with--> PV−`, weight 0.4. The span: 'the local pooling hypothesis PREDICTS that PV+ cells, LIKE PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. CONSISTENT WITH THIS, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells WERE NOT SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENT.' The sentence contains the word `like`, the phrase `consistent with this`, and a null - three signals that the two cell types are being shown to MATCH. The edge's own note says 'the contrast the paper looked for is absent, and its absence is the finding', and then asserts the contrast anyway. THE NULL RESULT HAD NOWHERE TO GO. The schema has `contrasted-with` and `distinct-from` for a difference and `same-as` for an identity, and NOTHING FOR 'THE DIFFERENCE WAS LOOKED FOR AND NOT FOUND'. So the nearest positive type was chosen, the truth was written into `note`, and `weight` was lowered - which is this project's own thesis committed inside its own layer: the missing vocabulary did not produce a gap in the data, IT PRODUCED A VALUE IN THE WRONG FIELD. A join reads the type; it does not read the note, and it cannot distinguish a low weight meaning 'weak evidence' from one meaning 'the opposite of what I said'. Q-388. — strength of the relation: 0.4 — the record marks this weak — WEIGHT LOW ON PURPOSE: tuning widths did NOT differ - the contrast the paper looked for is absent, and its absence is the finding
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: ChR2 —operationalised-as→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — identity is a light response, and the paper quantifies the tag both ways in two reporter lines
span.quote: More than 97% of PV+ cells expressed ChR2-eYFP, as indicated by fluorescent immunostaining for PV ( Fig. 1 b ; n = 657 cells in two mice, four sections total). YFP-fluorescent somata were difficult to distinguish from neuropil because the ChR2-eYFP fusion protein is membrane-bound. To better quantify the distribution of PV+ cells in auditory cortex we crossed Pvalb -IRES-Cre to a cre-dependent tdTomato reporter line ( Madisen et al., 2010 ). Expression specificity was similar for the cytosolic tdTomato reporter: >97% of tdTomato-expressing cells stained positively for PV; >96% of PV-positive cells expressed tdTomato ( Fig. 1 c ; n = 638 cells in one mouse, four sections).

span.label: waveform —distinct-from→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE PROXY MEASURED AGAINST A GENETIC GROUND TRUTH AND FOUND WANTING: up to 40 percent misclassification from any single waveform measure
span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons. These results suggest that both PV+ and FS cells are heterogeneous populations that overlap but are not identical.

span.label: FS —distinct-from→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the two are heterogeneous populations that OVERLAP BUT ARE NOT IDENTICAL - so results reported for one do not transfer to the other
span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons. These results suggest that both PV+ and FS cells are heterogeneous populations that overlap but are not identical.

span.label: spike width —operationalised-as→ FS
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the 0.8 ms cutoff is set from this dataset, and the paper says there is no consensus value because it depends on the recording technology
span.quote: To separate fast-spiking (FS) from regular-spiking (RS) cells based on spike width alone, we used an empirically determined value of 0.8 ms, which was approximately halfway between the mean spike widths of our PV+ and PV− groups and provided the best separation between them. There does not appear to be a consensus value for the extracellular FS/RS spike width cutoff in the literature ( Atencio and Schreiner, 2008 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Wu et al., 2008 ) because it may depend on the choice of recording technology.

span.label: PV+ —part-of→ basket cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.5 — the record marks this weak — and only approximately half of basket cells express PV, which is the second reason the waveform proxy cannot work
span.quote: Although narrow spikes are typical of PV+ inhibitory neurons, using extracellular waveforms to identify them in vivo may result in both type I and type II misclassification errors, for two reasons. First, although studies in wild-type animals support the general validity of extracellular spike duration as a proxy for intracellular duration, its reliability can vary depending on the size of the recorded neuron and its position relative to the electrode ( Henze et al., 2000 ; González-Burgos et al., 2005 ; Gold et al., 2006 ). Second, even using intracellular spikes, the FS/PV+ relationship is not one-to-one: not all PV+ cells have narrow spikes, nor do all narrow-spike cells express PV ( Gray and McCormick, 1996 ; Cauli et al., 2000 ; Markram et al., 2004 ). In fact, PV is expressed in only approximately half of basket cells

span.label: endslope —part-of→ waveform
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — three separate waveform measures, all differing at the population level and all overlapping at the cell level
span.quote: Despite these marked differences at the population level, the two groups showed appreciable overlap for all waveform measures, consistent with other in vivo studies ( Dykes et al., 1988 ; Nowak et al., 2003 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Liu et al., 2009 ). In our sample, 27/72 PV− neurons had narrow spikes (width < 0.8 ms, see Materials and Methods), 29/72 had negative endslopes, and 17/72 had peak/trough ratios <1.

span.label: untuned —distinct-from→ tuning width
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE MEASURE HAS A DOMAIN: a sound-responsive cell with disordered structure gets a label rather than a number
span.quote: For this untuned but sound-responsive neuron, a Gaussian fit provided a poor estimate of tuning width ( Fig. 2 d ; R 2 = 0.04); indeed, the notion of tuning width seems inappropriate to describe such a neuron, and we therefore categorized this neuron as untuned (UT).

span.label: lateral inhibition —distinct-from→ tuning width
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: the lateral account needs inhibitory neurons more broadly tuned than excitatory ones, and the measured widths do not differ
span.quote: Lateral inhibition models propose that inhibition sharpens spike tuning by specifically inhibiting responses to nonpreferred stimuli ( Calford and Semple, 1995 ; Chen and Jen, 2000 ; Sutter and Loftus, 2003 ). This could be implemented by PV+ neurons that are more broadly tuned than excitatory neurons ( Wu et al., 2008 ), but our finding that PV+ and PV− neurons have similar tuning widths is inconsistent with this model.

span.label: cotuning —causes→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the favoured model, produced by unbiased local connectivity, with only a moderate impact on frequency tuning
span.quote: Together, our results therefore favor a model of cotuning of PV+ neurons, produced by unbiased local connectivity, in which PV+-mediated inhibition has only a moderate impact on frequency tuning.

span.label: monotonicity index —operationalised-as→ intensity tuning
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — 1 means none and near zero means strong - the measure carries its own null
span.quote: Monotonicity index (MI) characterizes the strength of a cell's intensity tuning. We defined MI as the neuron's response at maximum intensity (90 dB) divided by its maximum response ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ). An MI of 1 indicates no intensity tuning; an MI near zero indicates very strong intensity tuning.

span.label: white noise —contrasted-with→ rate-level function
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — STIMULUS-DEPENDENT CONCLUSION: gain, dynamic range and monotonicity all separate the cell classes for tones at characteristic frequency and none of them do for white noise
span.quote: White noise rate-level functions (bottom) showed a different pattern of results: PV+ and PV− neurons were not significantly different in terms of response gain ( d , bottom), sound level dynamic range ( e , bottom), or monotonicity ( g , bottom).

span.label: latency —operationalised-as→ best frequency
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — latency is measured at the cell's own best frequency, so cells whose best frequency fell outside the speaker range are excluded from BOTH analyses
span.quote: We quantified the bandwidth of iso-intensity frequency tuning curves using σ of a Gaussian fit to the tuning curve. To ensure that σ was a good estimate of tuning width we excluded cells that were poorly fit by a Gaussian, using a criterion of R 2 < 0.2 (note that varying this value by ± 0.2 did not affect our results, even using a criterion of R 2 = 0, i.e., no cells excluded), or had a best frequency that exceeded the upper frequency range of our speakers (μ > 40 kHz). Because we could not confidently estimate the best frequency of these cells, we also excluded them from our analysis of response latency to tones at best frequency.

span.label: best frequency —distinct-from→ tuning width
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE INSTRUMENT BOUNDS THE SAMPLE: cells whose best frequency exceeded the speakers were dropped because the upper flank of the curve was truncated
span.quote: We quantified the bandwidth of iso-intensity frequency tuning curves using σ of a Gaussian fit to the tuning curve. To ensure that σ was a good estimate of tuning width we excluded cells that were poorly fit by a Gaussian, using a criterion of R 2 < 0.2 (note that varying this value by ± 0.2 did not affect our results, even using a criterion of R 2 = 0, i.e., no cells excluded), or had a best frequency that exceeded the upper frequency range of our speakers (μ > 40 kHz). Because we could not confidently estimate the best frequency of these cells, we also excluded them from our analysis of response latency to tones at best frequency.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE `to` ENDPOINT IS AN ADVERB) · auditory cortex —part-of→ tonotopically
span.note: RETRACTED: THE `to` ENDPOINT IS AN ADVERB. The edge is `auditory cortex --part-of--> tonotopically`. The span: 'Because MOUSE AUDITORY CORTEX IS TONOTOPICALLY ORGANIZED, the local pooling hypothesis predicts...' A cortex cannot be part of `tonotopically`. What the clause states is a PROPERTY of the cortex - that its organisation is tonotopic - and the tagger took the adverb as if it named a thing. Same shape as the `trend`, `terminology` and `classification` endpoints retracted earlier today: A WORD THAT IS NOT A NOUN PHRASE CANNOT BE AN ENDPOINT. Found by the neighbour query (Q-400). Q-423. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: Unless stated otherwise, statistical results are reported as mean ± SD and p value, compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Unless stated otherwise, statistical results are reported as mean ± SD and p value, compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test.

span.label: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
span.quote: The distribution of depths for our electrophysiologically recorded PV+ neurons did not differ significantly from the distribution of tdTomato-expressing cells (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p > 0.05), although neurons in deep layers were slightly underrepresented in our sample.

span.label: Fisher's exact test
span.quote: Similarly, when we categorized neurons as either monotonic or nonmonotonic using a criterion of MI = 0.5 ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ), only 14% of PV+ cells (7/48) were nonmonotonic, compared with 55% of PV− cells (21/38; p < 0.01, Fisher's exact test).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Moreover, PV+ cells in different layer groups did not differ significantly from one another for any of these measures ( p > 0.05, one-way ANOVA).

span.label: curve fitting (Gaussian)
span.quote: We quantified the bandwidth of iso-intensity frequency tuning curves using σ of a Gaussian fit to the tuning curve.

span.label: goodness of fit / coefficient of determination
span.term: goodness of fit / coefficient of determination
span.quote: We categorized neurons as either tuned or untuned based on the goodness of a Gaussian fit, using an arbitrary criterion of R 2 = 0.2 (varying this value by ± 0.2 did not affect our result, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Moreover, Δ dB was correlated with MI ( r = 0.377, p < 0.01), suggesting that the greater monotonicity of PV+ neurons is responsible for their increased dynamic range in sound level, and thus their comparatively shallow response gain.

span.label: resampling (random subsampling of trials)
span.quote: Response latency was the mean of the distribution of estimates from 1000 such subsamples.

span.label: parametric model fitting
span.quote: We fit each RLF with a six-parameter, two-tailed split Gaussian ( Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ).

span.label: Wilcoxon rank sum test
span.quote: PV+ cells indeed had narrower spikes than PV− cells ( Fig. 1 g ; PV+: 0.75 ± 0.18 ms, PV−: 0.93 ± 0.29 ms, p < 0.01).

span.label: two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
span.quote: The distribution of depths for our electrophysiologically recorded PV+ neurons did not differ significantly from the distribution of tdTomato-expressing cells (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p > 0.05), although neurons in deep layers were slightly underrepresented in our sample.

span.label: Frequency tuning width did not differ significantly between optogenetically identified PV+ interneurons and PV- neurons in mouse auditory cortex (0.84 vs 0.62 octaves), unlike the broad orientation tuning reported for PV+ cells in mouse visual cortex.
span.quote: Although PV+ cells were slightly more broadly tuned on average, the mean tuning widths of PV+ and PV− neurons were not significantly different (PV+: 0.84 ± 0.52 octaves, PV-: 0.62 ± 0.51 octaves, p = 0.06).

span.label: Very tightly tuned cells (below 0.5 octaves) were about half as common among PV+ cells (29%) as among PV- cells (58%), even though the two distributions largely overlapped.
span.quote: The tuning width distributions were largely overlapping ( Fig. 2 h ), although we noted that there were fewer “very tightly” tuned PV+ cells (σ < 0.5 octaves, 9/31, 29%) than PV− cells (20/34, 58%; p < 0.05, Fisher's exact test)

span.label: The best frequency of every tuned PV+ neuron was within half an octave of its recording site's best frequency, so PV+ tuning matched the local population.
span.quote: The best frequencies of all tuned PV+ neurons fell within one half octave of the best frequency of their recording sites, as estimated from multiunit or local field potential tuning curves (mean difference: 0.0 ± 0.1 octaves), indicating that the tuning of PV+ cells matched that of the local population.

span.label: PV+ cells responded to best-frequency tones roughly 11 ms earlier than PV- cells (17.9 vs 29.1 ms).
span.quote: PV+ cells had shorter response latencies than PV− cells ( Fig. 3 b , c ; PV+: 17.9 ± 5.9 ms, n = 31, PV−: 29.1 ± 10.9 ms, n = 34, p < 0.001), as measured at best frequency, 20 dB above threshold.

span.label: The latency advantage was stimulus-specific: for white noise, PV+ and PV- latencies did not differ significantly.
span.quote: Interestingly, response latencies to white noise were not significantly different (20 dB above white noise threshold, PV+: 22.0 ± 9.6 ms, n = 57; PV−: 25.9 ± 13.7 ms, n = 49, p > 0.05), possibly due to the high variability in PV− response latencies for white noise.

span.label: PV+ cells fired at twice the spontaneous rate (5.5 vs 2.0 Hz) and twice the sound-evoked rate (30.3 vs 14.5 Hz) of PV- cells.
span.quote: Consistent with reports from mouse visual cortex ( Liu et al., 2009 ; Atallah et al., 2012 ), PV+ cells had twofold higher spontaneous ( Fig. 3 a ; PV+: 5.5 ± 4.8 Hz n = 57, PV−: 2.0 ± 2.5 Hz n = 49, p < 0.01) and evoked firing rates

span.label: After normalizing for their higher firing rates, PV+ cells had shallower response gain to characteristic-frequency tones than PV- cells (0.04 vs 0.15).
span.quote: When we normalized CF rate-level functions for maximal evoked firing rate, PV+ neurons had a significantly shallower gain than PV− neurons ( Fig. 4 d , top; PV+: 0.04 ± 0.05, PV−:0.15 ± 0.24, p < 0.01).

span.label: PV+ cells were markedly less intensity-tuned than PV- cells for tones at characteristic frequency: only 14% of PV+ cells were nonmonotonic compared with 55% of PV- cells.
span.quote: Similarly, when we categorized neurons as either monotonic or nonmonotonic using a criterion of MI = 0.5 ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ), only 14% of PV+ cells (7/48) were nonmonotonic, compared with 55% of PV− cells (21/38; p < 0.01, Fisher's exact test).

span.label: For white noise, where the two groups were equally monotonic, the gain and dynamic-range differences disappeared, indicating the gain difference follows from monotonicity rather than being an independent property.
span.quote: When we used white noise to measure rate-level functions, we found that PV+ and PV− neurons were not significantly different in terms of monotonicity ( Fig. 4 g , bottom; PV+: 0.77 ± 0.21, n = 57, PV−: 0.67 ± 0.28, n = 49, p > 0.05).

span.label: Classifying cells by extracellular spike waveform instead of by PV expression would misclassify as many as 40% of them, so waveform is an unreliable marker of PV+ identity.
span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons.

span.label: The classification method changes the scientific conclusion: sorting the same cells by spike width rather than PV expression made narrow-spike cells come out significantly more broadly tuned than broad-spike cells (0.87 vs 0.60 octaves).
span.quote: Indeed, when we separated our cells according to spike width, rather than expression-type, we found that narrow-spike cells (width < 0.8 ms, n = 32) were significantly more broadly tuned than broad-spike cells ( n = 33; narrow-spike, FS: 0.87 ± 0.57 octaves; broad-spike, RS: 0.60 ± 0.44 octaves, p = 0.04).

span.label: All the PV+/PV- differences held separately within supragranular, granular and subgranular layers, and PV+ cells did not differ across layers.
span.quote: The differences reported above for PV+ and PV− cells across all layers were also true for PV+ and PV− cells within in these groups (Wilcoxon rank sum test, significance level = 0.05).

span.label: frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV- cells were not significantly different, as the local pooling account predicts for a tonotopic area
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: very tightly tuned PV+ cells were comparatively rare, which fits pooling over locally diverse tuning
span.quote: Although tonotopy is present on a large scale in mouse A1, the tuning of neighboring neurons can be diverse at a fine scale ( Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010 ; Rothschild et al., 2010 ). Consequently, unbiased local pooling would be unlikely to produce very narrowly tuned cells. Indeed, although the tuning width distributions were largely overlapping, there were comparatively few very tightly tuned PV+ cells in our sample

span.label: THE PREDICTION WAS DERIVED BEFORE THE TEST: if unbiased pooling generalises across modalities, PV+ cells should be well tuned here because auditory cortex has frequency columns
span.quote: If this principle generalizes across sensory modalities, PV+ neurons in mouse auditory cortex should be well tuned for frequency, because it has tonotopically organized frequency columns.

span.label: and the same principle explains why PV+ cells are broadly tuned in mouse V1, which lacks orientation columns
span.quote: Because PV+ neurons densely sample a small radius, their tuning is expected to reflect feature organization in local networks: in orientation columns in cat V1 and vibrissa barrels in rodent S1, PV+ cells will sample inputs with homogeneous tuning, and thus themselves will be well tuned ( Simons, 1978 ; Hirsch et al., 2003 ; Cardin et al., 2007 ; Nowak et al., 2008 ). In contrast, PV+ neurons are found to be poorly tuned where cells with different stimulus preferences are organized in a salt-and-pepper fashion, as in mouse V1, which lacks orientation columns

span.label: the tag was quantified in both directions and in two reporter lines: over 97 percent of PV-stained cells carried the opsin, and over 97 percent of reporter cells stained for PV
span.quote: More than 97% of PV+ cells expressed ChR2-eYFP, as indicated by fluorescent immunostaining for PV ( Fig. 1 b ; n = 657 cells in two mice, four sections total). YFP-fluorescent somata were difficult to distinguish from neuropil because the ChR2-eYFP fusion protein is membrane-bound. To better quantify the distribution of PV+ cells in auditory cortex we crossed Pvalb -IRES-Cre to a cre-dependent tdTomato reporter line ( Madisen et al., 2010 ). Expression specificity was similar for the cytosolic tdTomato reporter: >97% of tdTomato-expressing cells stained positively for PV; >96% of PV-positive cells expressed tdTomato ( Fig. 1 c ; n = 638 cells in one mouse, four sections).

span.label: A CONTAMINATION BOUND COMPUTED RATHER THAN ASSERTED: from under 1 percent pyramidal-morphology reporter cells and 24 of 68 recordings in layer V, the sample is estimated to contain fewer than 0.24 pyramidal neurons
span.quote: Parvalbumin is transiently expressed in a small subset of layer V pyramidal neurons during development ( Tanahira et al., 2009 ). Because Cre-mediated recombination is permanent, transient expression during development could lead to permanent ChR2 expression, even in cells that no longer express PV in adulthood. We did note that a very small subset (<1%) of tdTomato-expressing cells in layer V had pyramidal-type morphology. Of our sample of 68 recorded PV+ neurons, 24 were found in layer V (∼420–650 μm; Anderson et al., 2009 ) and we therefore estimate that our sample contained <0.24 pyramidal neurons. In other words, our PV+ neurons are almost certainly exclusively PV+ inhibitory interneurons.

span.label: PV+ cells did have narrower spikes, 0.75 against 0.93 ms
span.quote: PV+ cells indeed had narrower spikes than PV− cells ( Fig. 1 g ; PV+: 0.75 ± 0.18 ms, PV−: 0.93 ± 0.29 ms, p < 0.01).

span.label: but the distributions overlapped on every waveform measure: 27 of 72 PV- cells had narrow spikes, 29 had negative endslopes, 17 had low peak/trough ratios
span.quote: Despite these marked differences at the population level, the two groups showed appreciable overlap for all waveform measures, consistent with other in vivo studies ( Dykes et al., 1988 ; Nowak et al., 2003 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Liu et al., 2009 ). In our sample, 27/72 PV− neurons had narrow spikes (width < 0.8 ms, see Materials and Methods), 29/72 had negative endslopes, and 17/72 had peak/trough ratios <1.

span.label: THE PROXY QUANTIFIED AND REJECTED: any single waveform measure could misclassify up to 40 percent, and PV+ and FS are overlapping but non-identical populations
span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons. These results suggest that both PV+ and FS cells are heterogeneous populations that overlap but are not identical.

span.label: and there is no consensus spike-width cutoff in the literature, because it may depend on the recording technology
span.quote: To separate fast-spiking (FS) from regular-spiking (RS) cells based on spike width alone, we used an empirically determined value of 0.8 ms, which was approximately halfway between the mean spike widths of our PV+ and PV− groups and provided the best separation between them. There does not appear to be a consensus value for the extracellular FS/RS spike width cutoff in the literature ( Atencio and Schreiner, 2008 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Wu et al., 2008 ) because it may depend on the choice of recording technology.

span.label: two reasons the proxy cannot work: extracellular duration depends on cell size and electrode position, and even intracellularly the fast-spiking to PV relation is not one to one
span.quote: Although narrow spikes are typical of PV+ inhibitory neurons, using extracellular waveforms to identify them in vivo may result in both type I and type II misclassification errors, for two reasons. First, although studies in wild-type animals support the general validity of extracellular spike duration as a proxy for intracellular duration, its reliability can vary depending on the size of the recorded neuron and its position relative to the electrode ( Henze et al., 2000 ; González-Burgos et al., 2005 ; Gold et al., 2006 ). Second, even using intracellular spikes, the FS/PV+ relationship is not one-to-one: not all PV+ cells have narrow spikes, nor do all narrow-spike cells express PV ( Gray and McCormick, 1996 ; Cauli et al., 2000 ; Markram et al., 2004 ). In fact, PV is expressed in only approximately half of basket cells

span.label: SOME CELLS GOT A LABEL INSTEAD OF A NUMBER: 6 of 46 in each group were sound-responsive but had no meaningful tuning width
span.quote: For this untuned but sound-responsive neuron, a Gaussian fit provided a poor estimate of tuning width ( Fig. 2 d ; R 2 = 0.04); indeed, the notion of tuning width seems inappropriate to describe such a neuron, and we therefore categorized this neuron as untuned (UT).

span.label: the untuned criterion was declared arbitrary and varying it by plus or minus 0.2 did not change the result
span.quote: We categorized neurons as either tuned or untuned based on the goodness of a Gaussian fit, using an arbitrary criterion of R 2 = 0.2 (varying this value by ± 0.2 did not affect our result, see Materials and Methods). By this criterion, 6/46 PV+ and 6/46 PV− cells were untuned and we excluded these cells from our tuning width analysis. The prevalence of untuned neurons was identical in our PV+ and PV− samples, and they showed no difference from tuned neurons in terms of spike width, spontaneous firing rate, or cortical depth.

span.label: further cells were dropped when best frequency exceeded the speaker range, leaving 31 PV+ and 34 PV- for tuning width
span.quote: Of the tuned cells, we excluded 9/40 PV+ cells and 6/40 PV− cells with best frequencies outside the frequency range of our speaker, because this truncated the upper flank of the tuning curve and we could not confidently measure their tuning width. This resulted in a sample of 31 PV+ and 34 PV− neurons for which we could estimate tuning width with high confidence.

span.label: NO A PRIORI LATENCY CONSTRAINTS, and imposing several exclusion criteria afterwards did not change the results
span.quote: We did not impose any a priori constraints on latency values. Imposing exclusion criteria, such as the SD of the distribution exceeding 10 ms (CF: 6/31 PV+, 6/34 PV− excluded; WN: 9/57 PV+, 10/49 PV− excluded) or even 5 ms (CF: 10/31 PV+, 18/34 PV−; WN: 29/57 PV+, 21/49 PV−) did not change our results.

span.label: and the latency result was confirmed with an alternative estimation method
span.quote: We confirmed our results using an alternative latency estimation method.

span.label: PV+ neurons had markedly faster response latencies, read as feedforward inhibition driven by thalamocortical excitation
span.quote: We found that PV+ neurons had markedly faster response latencies than PV− neurons. These very short latencies suggest that PV+ neurons participate in a feedforward inhibitory network that is rapidly activated by thalamocortical excitation, and likely underlies the sequence of early synaptic excitation and inhibition seen in whole-cell recordings from pyramidal neurons

span.label: PV+ rate-level functions were more monotonic at characteristic frequency, supporting a role in shaping intensity tuning
span.quote: We found that PV+ neurons were highly monotonic for pure tones at their characteristic frequency compared with PV− neurons. This supports the idea that local inhibition shapes intensity tuning in auditory cortex, and that it is provided at least in part by PV+ neurons.

span.label: STIMULUS-DEPENDENT: for white noise, gain, dynamic range and monotonicity did not separate the two classes at all
span.quote: White noise rate-level functions (bottom) showed a different pattern of results: PV+ and PV− neurons were not significantly different in terms of response gain ( d , bottom), sound level dynamic range ( e , bottom), or monotonicity ( g , bottom).

span.label: the broadly-tuned-inhibition version of lateral inhibition is inconsistent with equal tuning widths
span.quote: Lateral inhibition models propose that inhibition sharpens spike tuning by specifically inhibiting responses to nonpreferred stimuli ( Calford and Semple, 1995 ; Chen and Jen, 2000 ; Sutter and Loftus, 2003 ). This could be implemented by PV+ neurons that are more broadly tuned than excitatory neurons ( Wu et al., 2008 ), but our finding that PV+ and PV− neurons have similar tuning widths is inconsistent with this model.

span.label: and the far-projecting version is inconsistent with PV+ tuning matching the local field potential and with equal connectivity spread
span.quote: Alternatively, lateral inhibition could be provided by well tuned PV+ neurons that project farther laterally than excitatory projections do. These PV+ neurons would have tuning complementary to that of their excitatory targets. This model would be consistent with our results for tuning width, but inconsistent with our finding that PV+ tuning matches that of the local population, as well as with a recent study in mouse auditory cortex that found that the spatial spread of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal connectivity was the same

span.label: so the results favour cotuning with only moderate impact on frequency tuning
span.quote: Together, our results therefore favor a model of cotuning of PV+ neurons, produced by unbiased local connectivity, in which PV+-mediated inhibition has only a moderate impact on frequency tuning.

span.label: though lateral inhibition remains possible through a different network configuration or through other inhibitory cell types
span.quote: Nevertheless, lateral inhibition could still be implemented in auditory cortex in at least two ways. First, recent modeling studies have shown that a single network architecture (which is consistent with our results) can operate in either a cotuned or lateral inhibition configuration, depending on the strength and spatial profile of thalamic input ( Levy and Reyes, 2011 ). Second, other inhibitory cell types could participate in classical lateral inhibition.

span.label: A DISSOCIATION BETWEEN THE GENETIC AND PHYSIOLOGICAL CLASSES: tuning was equal for PV+ and PV- but slightly broader for FS cells, hinting at two distinct inhibitory networks
span.quote: Both mechanisms moderately sharpen tuning; the first predicts that excitatory and inhibitory neurons will have similar tuning, the second predicts that inhibitory neurons will be slightly more broadly tuned. We observed similar tuning for PV+ and PV− cells, but slightly broader tuning for FS cells ( Fig. 2 j ), suggesting the possibility that these two mechanisms may be implemented by distinct inhibitory networks.

span.label: well tuned PV+ cells would also follow from selective connectivity, which the data cannot exclude
span.quote: We note that well tuned PV+ neurons are also consistent with selective connectivity rather than unbiased pooling, because narrow tuning could follow from either scheme. However, this would represent a different connectivity rule than is found in other cortical areas.

span.label: the recorded depth distribution matched the anatomical one, with deep layers slightly underrepresented
span.quote: The distribution of depths for our electrophysiologically recorded PV+ neurons did not differ significantly from the distribution of tdTomato-expressing cells (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p > 0.05), although neurons in deep layers were slightly underrepresented in our sample.

span.label: monotonicity index (MI)
span.quote: We defined MI as the neuron's response at maximum intensity (90 dB) divided by its maximum response ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ).

span.label: characteristic frequency (CF)
span.quote: To determine each neuron's characteristic frequency (CF; the frequency that evoked spikes at the lowest sound level) we first obtained a coarse frequency-intensity tuning curve (1–40 kHz at 4 frequencies/octave, 20–80 dB in 15 dB steps, ≤10 repetitions).

span.label: response gain
span.quote: We first looked for differences in response gain, which we defined as the relationship between sound level (input) and the cell's spiking response (output).

span.label: endslope
span.quote: The latter is the slope of the waveform 0.5 ms after the trough.

span.label: untuned (UT) cell
span.quote: We categorized neurons as either tuned or untuned based on the goodness of a Gaussian fit, using an arbitrary criterion of R 2 = 0.2 (varying this value by ± 0.2 did not affect our result, see Materials and Methods).

span.label: monotonicity index
span.quote: Monotonicity index (MI) characterizes the strength of a cell's intensity tuning. We defined MI as the neuron's response at maximum intensity (90 dB) divided by its maximum response ( Sutter and Schreiner, 1995 ; de la Rocha et al., 2008 ; Watkins and Barbour, 2011 ). An MI of 1 indicates no intensity tuning; an MI near zero indicates very strong intensity tuning.

span.label: untuned
span.quote: For this untuned but sound-responsive neuron, a Gaussian fit provided a poor estimate of tuning width ( Fig. 2 d ; R 2 = 0.04); indeed, the notion of tuning width seems inappropriate to describe such a neuron, and we therefore categorized this neuron as untuned (UT).

span.label: FS
span.quote: To separate fast-spiking (FS) from regular-spiking (RS) cells based on spike width alone, we used an empirically determined value of 0.8 ms, which was approximately halfway between the mean spike widths of our PV+ and PV− groups and provided the best separation between them. There does not appear to be a consensus value for the extracellular FS/RS spike width cutoff in the literature ( Atencio and Schreiner, 2008 ; Niell and Stryker, 2008 ; Wu et al., 2008 ) because it may depend on the choice of recording technology.

span.label: cotuning
span.quote: More recently, voltage-clamp studies have shown that excitation and inhibition are instead cotuned for frequency and approximately fixed in their relative proportions ( Wehr and Zador, 2003 ; Zhang et al., 2003 ; Tan et al., 2004 ; for review see Oswald et al., 2006 ). In the cotuning model, inhibition moderately sharpens spike tuning through a thresholding or “iceberg” mechanism, scaling down depolarization across the same range of frequencies as excitation.

span.label: cell class (PV+ vs PV-, set by optogenetic tagging)
span.term: cell class (PV+ vs PV-, set by optogenetic tagging)
span.quote: To gain insight into their computational role, here we ask whether and how the response properties of PV+ neurons differ from those of PV− neurons, which are primarily excitatory pyramidal cells.

span.label: sound intensity
span.quote: To measure rate-level functions, we presented WN and/or pure tones at CF at intensities of −10 to 90 dB in 5 dB steps (or in a few cases, 10 dB steps from 0 to 80 dB).

span.label: tone frequency
span.quote: Iso-intensity tuning curves consisted of pure tones from 1 to 40 kHz, sampled at 6 frequencies/octave.

span.label: frequency tuning width (sigma of Gaussian fit)
span.term: frequency tuning width (sigma of Gaussian fit)
span.quote: We quantified the bandwidth of iso-intensity frequency tuning curves using σ of a Gaussian fit to the tuning curve.

span.label: response latency
span.quote: We computed response latency for pure tones at best frequency and white noise, 20 dB above threshold.

span.label: sound-evoked firing rate
span.quote: Responses were computed as the spike rate in an 80 ms window following sound onset and averaged across all presentations (typically 20) of the stimulus.

span.label: stimulus level held at 20 dB above each cell's own threshold
span.term: stimulus level held at 20 dB above each cell's own threshold
span.quote: We then used this value, the CF pure-tone threshold, to select the appropriate level for an iso-intensity tuning curve, which was presented 20 dB above threshold.

span.label: maximal evoked firing rate (normalized out of the gain comparison)
span.term: maximal evoked firing rate (normalized out of the gain comparison)
span.quote: We therefore normalized rate-level functions to control for the higher firing rates in PV+ neurons.

span.label: cortical recording depth (matched across groups)
span.quote: Our PV+ and PV− groups had similar depth distributions (PV+: 442 ± 184 μm, PV−: 396 ± 175 μm, p > 0.05; mean ± SD, Wilcoxon Rank-sum for this and subsequent tests).

span.label: tuning width
span.quote: Because mouse auditory cortex is tonotopically organized, the local pooling hypothesis predicts that PV+ cells, like PV− cells, will be well tuned to an area's preferred frequency. Consistent with this, we found that the frequency tuning widths of PV+ and PV− cells were not significantly different.

span.label: latency
span.quote: We found that PV+ neurons had markedly faster response latencies than PV− neurons. These very short latencies suggest that PV+ neurons participate in a feedforward inhibitory network that is rapidly activated by thalamocortical excitation, and likely underlies the sequence of early synaptic excitation and inhibition seen in whole-cell recordings from pyramidal neurons

span.label: n = 68 — PV+ interneurons identified in vivo by their short-latency responses to blue light

span.quote: Separating these neurons according to any one waveform measure could therefore result in a misclassification rate of up to 40%, suggesting that extracellular waveforms are not reliable markers of PV+ neurons.

span.quote: Indeed, for pure tone stimuli at CF, mean MI was significantly higher for PV+ cells ( Fig. 4 g , top; PV+: 0.76 ± 0.22, PV−: 0.55 ± 0.28, p < 0.01), indicating that PV+ neurons are more monotonic than PV− neurons.

span.quote: Indeed, PV+ neurons had a significantly greater dynamic range in firing rate ( Fig. 4 c , Δ FR; PV+: 21.1 ± 18.3 Hz, PV−: 8.6 ± 6.5 Hz, p < 0.01).

span.label: 32 ± 18 dB / 19 ± 15 dB — sound-level dynamic range over which firing rate kept increasing, PV+ versus PV-
span.quote: In other words, their responses increased over a greater range of sound intensities ( Fig. 4 e, top, Δ dB; PV+: 32 ± 18 dB, PV−: 19 ± 15 dB, p < 0.01).
